title: UK FCA exec wants to require disclosure of ‘significant AI failures and near-misses’
raw_text: When UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Chief Data Officer Jessica Rusu gave a speech on Monday advocating that UK companies be required to report “significant AI failures and near-misses,” she added to the drumbeat of demands for some kind of regulatory control over enterprise AI deployments. But her speech also highlighted regulator frustration over futile attempts to slow down the seemingly unstoppable agentic and genAI rollouts, as reports of agent misbehavior and the lack of meaningful consequences continue to emerge with alarming frequency. Rusu , speaking to a Bloomberg UK Policy Series audience, said that firms need to invest more in cyber and operational resilience. “Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognized, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too,” Rusu said . “It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress, or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.” She added, “the FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators, and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.” One of the questions that came out of the speech is what precisely was meant by “significant AI failures and near-misses.” Questions to FCA to clarify their terminology were not answered by publication time. AI failure vs near miss But Pieter Arntz , a malware intelligence researcher at security firm Malwarebytes, offered his own take on what those terms likely mean. “A significant AI failure is one with serious consequences, not simply an incorrect answer. In financial services, that could mean an AI system authorizing substantial fraudulent payments, exposing sensitive customer information, denying customers access to essential financial services, or triggering transactions that threaten market integrity,” Arntz said. “The test should be the scale and severity of the impact, rather than whether the failure looks technically dramatic.” On the other hand, he added, “An AI near-miss is an event that could realistically have caused serious harm, but was caught before that harm occurred. For example, an AI agent might attempt an unauthorized transfer that a separate approval control blocks, or a prompt-injection attack might induce it to disclose sensitive information, only for an outbound security control to stop the disclosure.” However, Arntz warned of the risk to Rusu’s approach, should the final penalties be underwhelming. “There is a risk of this becoming a paper tiger if compliance amounts to filing a report and absorbing a predictable fine,” he said. Warnings from multiple directions UK-based Gartner VP analyst Nader Henein said he is skeptical about the significance of the FCA’s proposal, in part because so many UK enterprises already have to comply with EU regulations, which have started asking companies to make such disclosures. “Financial watchdogs including the Bank of England (BoE), the UAE Central Bank, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore have all issued warnings,” he said. “A few months ago, the European central banks, together with the European Systemic Risk Board, escalated the cyber risk assessment level associated with frontier models to ‘severe,’ warning that simultaneous cyber incidents could impact the financial sector. They acknowledged that AI-driven cyber incidents now threaten core financial sector stability.” Henein said that he is especially skeptical that meaningful changes will occur in the financial sector. “Financial institutions tend to heed the warnings of the regulator that decides whether they can continue to operate, but without clear laws, regulatory oversight, and the obligatory fines, these disjointed statements are not likely to make a difference,” he said. Could ‘incentivize the wrong behavior’ Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, added that one risk of this increased visibility requirement is that it could inadvertently incentivize the wrong behavior. “A bank with good monitoring may catch hundreds of attempts by AI agents to act outside their authority,” he said. “A bank with poor monitoring may report zero, because it never saw them. On paper, the safer bank looks worse. A model failing a red-team test is the test working, not a regulatory incident.” However, Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, said that the near-miss approach has the strongest potential to change the conversation. “I love the near-miss idea. It is the most important thing in the speech. It is the part financial firms are least ready for,” he said. But, he stressed, “[Rusu] also warns about reliance on a single model. An outage at one AI supplier that takes down a customer service channel counts, too.” Another concern about reliance on a specific model is the ever-present risk that an AI vendor could change the model without telling all of its customers. “A model can pass testing in March and misbehave in May without anyone at the firm changing a line of code, because the provider changed the model underneath,” Dickson said. “A model version change should get the same scrutiny as any other production change.” This article originally appeared on CIO.com .

title: KVM escape exposes broader attack surface in Linux networking
raw_text: Security researchers have found a critical flaw in the Linux kernel’s networking stack that can let attackers escape a KVM virtual machine and execute code on the host system. The weakness could also potentially let attackers compromise systems running other Linux-based virtualization and sandbox platforms. Tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and dubbed PwnEscape , the vulnerability was discovered by researchers from AI-powered pentesting startup Pwn.ai during a $1 million challenge to hack Vercel’s sandbox platform , which uses KVM-based Firecracker microVMs. Rather than exploiting a bug in the KVM hypervisor itself, the attack targets the Linux networking code that handles traffic from inside virtual machines. Specially crafted packets can alter an IPv4 header after the host’s kernel has already validated it, causing later processing to trust packet data that attackers have manipulated. The Pwn.ai researchers demonstrated host-memory leakage against Vercel’s production sandboxes and separately achieved host crashes and root-level code execution on researcher-controlled systems. Vercel confirmed the findings but said no reports showed access to customer files, secrets, or application data. A fix was merged into the mainline Linux kernel with patched kernel versions now available for multiple distributions. Administrators need to deploy those kernel updates on host systems because updating only guest VMs does not fix the vulnerability. Checksum processing rewrites validated headers The flaw involves checksum offloading, a performance optimization that allows Linux to postpone calculating a packet’s checksum. Alongside the packet, the kernel carries metadata specifying where that calculation should begin and where its result should be written, but in virtual networking those instructions can originate from an untrusted guest. The vulnerable implementation failed to ensure that completing the checksum would leave the already-validated IPv4 header untouched, meaning that guest-controlled metadata could directly write into that header, changing the advertised length before the packet was split into smaller fragments for transmission. In their demonstration, the researchers managed to change the header length from 20 to 60 bytes, while the packet buffer held only 28 bytes of valid data. The fragmentation process then copied 32 bytes beyond that valid data into outgoing packets, leaking host memory. By repeating the process, the researchers were able to make observations and control memory allocations to achieve host-kernel memory writes to run a helper program as root. The complete exploitation steps that take this attack from a memory leak to code execution have not been publicly revealed yet, but the researchers plan a separate write-up. “The allocator-sensitive write chain, object-lifetime controls, and other hypervisor-specific adaptation are large enough to require a separate article,” they said. “Although we suspect the security industry will use this post to figure out the other affected hypervisors and we expect exploits in weaker configurations to arrive in weeks, and exploits working in default hypervisor configurations to arrive in under a month.” The attack surface extends beyond KVM PwnEscape differs from other VM escape attacks that target the hypervisor’s handling of virtual CPUs or memory. The Januscape vulnerability disclosed earlier this year , for example, affected KVM’s memory-management code, but with this exploit the vulnerable code is in the Linux host’s IPv4 networking subsystem. The researchers warn that similar bugs could exist elsewhere in the networking stack, wherever guest-controlled metadata can modify packet fields after those fields have already passed validation. The accepted patch , authored by Red Hat developer Michael S. Tsirkin, adds validation at five checksum completion points, including IPv4 fragmentation, bridge connection tracking, and packet filtering, but the patch commit message states that “a more complete validation at input is forthcoming, but needs more work.” The flaw’s impact for other hypervisors and container technologies remains to be seen. Red Hat lists OpenShift Container Platform components as affected , but other virtualization technologies like Docker or Xen have not issued advisories yet. The guest-to-host attack requires an attacker-controlled workload capable of supplying the malformed traffic through the virtual network. As a result, admins of environments that allow the execution of untrusted code inside VMs need to take action as soon as possible. “A VM escape is another kernel vulnerability because KVM lives inside the Linux kernel, but it has more serious implications,” Alex Zenla, CTO and co-founder of container security firm Edera, told CSO. “When a guest breaks out, it isn’t escaping into some neatly contained hypervisor; it can land in the lowest levels of the operating system that owns the host’s processes, drivers, and network stack. This is critical and a very different security proposition from a hypervisor designed with a deliberately tiny privileged layer.” KVM and other kernel-based virtualization components have had multiple critical vulnerabilities this year, some of them found with the help of LLMs, including PwnEscape. Meanwhile AI agents have been observed attempting to break out of sandboxes during tests. This challenges the workload isolation assumptions in virtualized environments. “Security architecture has to assume that eventually, something will be compromised and make sure that compromise doesn’t become total host ownership,” Zenla said. AWS says its managed EC2, Lambda, and Fargate services are unaffected by CVE-2026-99999, but customers running their own KVM virtual machines with virtio-net networking on vulnerable hosts need to apply the relevant kernel updates. Administrators should follow their distribution’s advisories because the fixes can be backported to older kernel versions.

The weakness could also potentially let attackers compromise systems running other Linux-based virtualization and sandbox platforms. Tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and dubbed PwnEscape , the vulnerability was discovered by researchers from AI-powered pentesting startup Pwn.ai during a $1 million challenge to hack Vercel’s sandbox platform , which uses KVM-based Firecracker microVMs. Rather than exploiting a bug in the KVM hypervisor itself, the attack targets the Linux networking code that handles traffic from inside virtual machines.

title: When defrost becomes sabotage: 3 OT lessons from France’s supermarket attack
raw_text: On the night of 11 October, someone remotely put the cold cases of several hundred French supermarkets into defrost. At Intermarché and Netto stores, fridges and freezers warmed to around 50°C and stayed there for about six hours, according to Les Mousquetaires, which expects losses in the tens of millions of euros. By morning, staff were filling skips with meat, frozen goods and vegetables. Coopérative U counted 80 affected stores out of roughly 2,000. Its chief executive, Dominique Schelcher, told RTL that the cold chain held in most of them. Only a minority reacted too slowly and lost stock, and he credited store staff and refrigeration contractors for the difference. Intermarché said its affected stores had to throw away everything. A second wave followed in the night of 12 to 13 October, this time also reaching stores with Dixell controllers. Similar controllers, similar night, very different mornings. That gap is the part of this story an operator can act on. CSO has already reported which systems were hit and what CERT-FR wants done with them. Nobody has claimed responsibility and no ransom demand has surfaced, which Reuters reports has puzzled investigators; whoever did this wanted spoiled food, not money, or has not said what they wanted yet. Neither CERT-FR nor Danfoss has said how the attackers got in: exposed management interfaces, known flaws and stolen contractor credentials are all still on the table. The three lessons that follow do not depend on either answer. Your refrigeration contractor is your perimeter Schelcher made a remark that deserves more attention than the temperature figures: Coopérative U stores do not buy from Danfoss. They buy from refrigeration contractors, who supply the controller, configure it and keep remote access to it so they can adjust setpoints without driving to the store. E.Leclerc told AFP that the attack reached its stores through one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers. The controller’s embedded web server exists for exactly this purpose, and the contractor’s performance guarantees usually depend on the data feed it provides. Danfoss has seen this before. Its own technical newsletter from October 2025 records attacks on the AK-SM 800 in 2022: 16 Russian supermarkets and 40 Israeli stores. All 40 Israeli sites, the newsletter notes, lacked proper firewall or VPN protection. Four years later the same model, end-of-life since May 2021, was still on the internet in France. The pattern is familiar from industrial sites. The party who decides whether a controller is exposed is not the party who eats the loss when it is. The contractor wants a browser and a public IP address because it turns a Sunday-night callout into a two-minute job. The store carries the inventory. A standard maintenance contract rarely makes that trade-off visible to the person signing it. How deep the dependency runs shows in a sentence I have not seen in a national advisory before. CERT-FR’s alert , updated on 16 October, tells operators to check their insurance terms before cutting the internet link to the refrigeration contractor. The data feed is contractual, and depending on the agreement, cutting it can touch monitoring obligations or policy conditions. And the insurance side is bleak anyway: brokers and underwriters told Reuters that cyber policies typically exclude physical loss, so the spoiled stock is unlikely to be covered. Intermarché told AFP its insurance does not cover the incident. So, the first question: who can log into your refrigeration controllers today, and over what path? Store network, contractor VPN, a cellular router the contractor installed years ago, a port forward on the store router? If answering requires calling the contractor, you do not control that perimeter. You rent it. The lesson is a contract clause, not a firewall rule. The maintenance agreement should name every remote path into the equipment and forbid any other; require access through your gateway or VPN with accounts tied to named technicians; give you the logs; oblige the contractor to tell you when a controller leaves vendor support or a vulnerability is published; and let you revoke access without losing the cold chain. Cold-case controllers run for decades. The contract that pays for their maintenance rarely says any of this. After France, it should. Defrost is a feature. Treat the command as the event Whatever got the attackers in, the damage itself came from ordinary refrigeration functions. Defrost is a built-in cycle on every refrigeration controller, and in the second wave the setpoints were reportedly pushed to values no case can reach. Many controllers also offer a setting that suppresses temperature alarms during defrost and for a delay afterwards, so that scheduled cycles do not page anyone at 3 a.m. That is a sensible configuration. It is also exactly what makes a forced defrost quiet. Whether it played a role in France has not been established, and Coopérative U’s experience shows that alarms did reach people in most of its stores. The structure is the same as in the Minnesota water attacks in July : intended functionality, used by the wrong person at the wrong time. A temperature alarm is a process control. It tells you the product is getting warm. It cannot tell you that the command which made it warm came from someone who should not have been logged in. The signal worth alarming on is an unexpected mode or setpoint change outside a maintenance window, and it gets louder when several circuits move at once or several stores that share a contractor move in the same hour. CERT-FR’s updated alert now tells operators to review their defrost schedules specifically. That is the right instinct: look at the configuration, not just the thermometer. Not every controller can export that event, least of all the models that were hit. Where it cannot, an independent temperature logger that does not depend on the controller catches the consequence early. Either way, someone has to receive the alert, understand it and have the authority to act. At 3 a.m. that chain runs from a store employee to an external technician to a central operations desk, and if nobody has written down who calls whom, the minutes go to finding out. In the second wave, a refrigeration technician in the Gironde told Le Monde that his teams reached a store near Bordeaux in time, and nothing had to be thrown away. Schelcher’s minority lost their stock because they could not respond fast enough. One factor clearly separated the two groups: time from first actionable warning to intervention. The lesson, concretely: an alert on any remote setpoint or mode change that no technician has announced, weighted by time of day and by how many circuits move together, raised by the controller where it can and by the contractor’s monitoring platform where it cannot, since the contractor is the only party that sees all its stores at once. A temperature logger that does not share the controller’s network, as the second opinion. A written call chain for 3 a.m. with names, not roles. And a drill: have the contractor change a setpoint on a test circuit at night and measure how many minutes pass before someone with authority has it reversed. That number is the one to report to the board. An unsupported controller is a budget line, not a patch ticket Claroty’s Team82 published three flaws in the current model , the AK-SM 800A, in August, all fixed in firmware 4.3.1 or earlier, and counted 2,765 of its management interfaces reachable from the internet. Nobody has linked those flaws to the attack. Danfoss says most affected units were the older AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355, with some 800A units on outdated firmware. For the older models, there is nothing to patch. Danfoss ended updates for the AK-SM 800 in May 2021 and for the AK-SC 355 in 2016. CERT-FR therefore does not lead with patching. It tells operators to take every AK-SM, AK-SC and XWEB controller off the public internet, restore access only through a VPN or protected network, and for compromised Danfoss units, restart, or failing that, factory-reset, and reconfigure before returning them to service. It adds a warning that reads like a prediction: a reset alone removes persistence but leaves the device just as vulnerable, and the campaign is probably still running. The sequence is the one I argued for when CISA asked operators to harden Siemens S7 PLCs : exposure first, firmware second, replacement third. In practice, that means a list of every refrigeration controller by model, firmware and vendor support status by the end of this week; a management interface on a public IP address taken off it the same day; current firmware on everything the vendor still supports; and for everything it does not, a replacement date with a budget line and a name next to it. An aging controller may still do its job perfectly well, and replacing it costs money, engineering time and downtime, so without an owner the decision slides. The security team can document the risk. Someone on the commercial side has to accept it or fund the replacement, and after Reuters’ insurance round-up, that person should know they are also accepting the stock. Which brings the story back to the two groups of stores. Nobody has shown that firmware or hardware explains which stores kept their stock. What is documented is that a warning reached someone who could act before the cold chain gave way. That is an operational capability, and it can be tested long before an attacker tests it for you. Sekoia told Reuters that Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium saw cases too, and the same controller families run cold storage in warehouses and pharmaceutical distribution, maintained by the same kind of contractor. So, before the week is out, do two things. Search Shodan or Censys for your own refrigeration management interfaces, because someone else already has. Then call the contractor and ask one question: when you log into our sites, how do you get there? If the answer is a public IP address and a password, with nothing in between, you have found your incident. It just hasn’t happened yet.
summary: On the night of 11 October, someone remotely put the cold cases of several hundred French supermarkets into defrost. At Intermarché and Netto stores, fridges and freezers warmed to around 50°C and stayed there for about six hours, according to Les Mousquetaires, which expects losses in the tens of millions of euros. By morning, staff were filling skips with meat, frozen goods and vegetables. Coopérative U counted 80 affected stores out of roughly 2,000.

title: OT systems complicate quantum-resistant data protection
raw_text: Quantum-resistant cryptography presents security leaders with various challenges, but CISOs in industries dependent on IoT and operational technology (OT) devices may face a particularly difficult journey to quantum readiness, especially if sensitive information that must remain confidential for years passes through those devices. A recent report from cybersecurity firm Forescout highlights these challenges in the healthcare industry, where medical histories, diagnostic images, and laboratory results, which retain their sensitivity long after they are created, routinely get transferred between various operational systems. Attackers who collect encrypted traffic carrying this information today can store it for decryption when sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available, an approach security experts call “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL). “PQC [post-quantum cryptography] migration in healthcare is not just about data confidentiality, but also patient safety,” the Forescout researchers say in their report, which examined over 2.5 million devices across more than 50 organizations. “Cryptography protects commands sent to medical devices, telemetry received from those devices for diagnostic purposes, medication orders, and other sensitive interactions. Quantum threats include unauthorized remote access by exploiting public keys for authentication, tampering with device-to-device communication by decrypting traffic, and sophisticated malware exploiting firmware integrity signatures.” While upgrading to PQC is relatively straightforward for live servers, where a standardized PQC algorithm can be implemented as a library package upgrade and configuration change, embedded devices such as those used in healthcare need full firmware updates from their manufacturers. Moreover, those upgrades must maintain backwards compatibility with other systems that might not be upgraded at the same time, and in the case of certified devices, they might require re-certification. This issue goes beyond healthcare to include industrial installations or anywhere OT or IoT devices handle sensitive or business-critical data. Last month, the G7 Cybersecurity Working Group urged governments and organizations to begin migrating to PQC as soon as possible, calling for action across all sectors. The group warned that the transition will be lengthy and that organizations should prepare before quantum computers capable of breaking current cryptography become available. Daniel dos Santos, VP of research at Forescout, tells CSO that while government bodies have issued orders and advisories with different expectations for PQC readiness, they all tend to converge on a 2030 timeline, which is when experts expect quantum computers might be capable of breaking existing encryption algorithms. For industries such as healthcare, however, the HNDL threat collapses that quantum-readiness timeline completely. Patient data travels beyond the medical device Protecting patient information requires securing the entire communication chain, from the equipment that generates the data to the IT systems that store it and the applications that make it available to doctors and patients. That includes, for example, a CT scanner that sends images to a picture archiving and communication system (PACS), images that can later be transferred between hospitals, cloud services, and external radiology providers, requiring quantum-resistant protection on each transfer to maintain long-term confidentiality. Laboratory results and prescription records follow similar routes. Electronic prescribing services exchange medication information between providers and pharmacies, including records of controlled substances and treatment for chronic diseases. Attackers can potentially intercept and siphon that data at different points in the chain: at the device level, from an internal network, through a compromised edge router or firewall, or even at the telecom operator’s level . The platforms that store and exchange patient records are often accessible directly from the internet as well. In a Shodan search, Forescout identified more than 5,500 internet-exposed instances of medical information systems, with electronic medical record platforms accounting for 46% of those instances and PACS accounting for 40%. Only 36% of PACS, 33% of electronic medical record systems, and 13% of laboratory information management systems had support for TLS 1.3, the only version of the protocol that supports ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism), a quantum-resistant key encapsulation standard published by NIST. However, the presence of TLS 1.3 does not demonstrate that a connection uses quantum-resistant cryptography, because the connecting client might negotiate a different algorithm. Furthermore, in a previous study published in June , Forescout found that only 11.8% of SSH servers on the internet are PQC-capable, a number that falls to 3% when looking only at Dropbear, an SSH server commonly used on embedded devices. Inside enterprise networks, 50% of IT devices use OpenSSH versions that support PQC, but only 28% of IoT, 16% of OT, and 6% of IoMT devices use the same versions. “Specialized devices are unlikely to be fully migrated this decade if we keep going at the current pace, delaying broader PQC migration efforts and quantum readiness,” the researchers concluded. “Unfortunately, medical devices are among those with the lowest adoption rates and the hardest challenges for adopting PQC.” Challenges extend beyond healthcare Changing cryptography on equipment used for patient care or industrial operations is completely dependent on the device vendor. Dos Santos says modifying the device filesystem independently, even when it can be done, jeopardizes certification, maintenance, and support, and any communication protocol changes need to preserve connections to other equipment. The same problem exists for devices in chemical plants, electricity networks, water treatment facilities, and factory floors. Some medical and industrial equipment already runs on Linux, which could in theory make adopting PQC easier, dos Santos says. However, he has seen little discussion of PQC adoption or roadmaps among OT vendors. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) described in its October 2024 OT guidance how changes to equipment controlling heavy machinery or combustible materials can require extensive safety testing. For medical devices, the regulatory implications depend on the changes made to the device. The US Food and Drug Administration’s February 2026 cybersecurity guidance says changes to authentication or encryption algorithms may require a new premarket submission. Concerns about legacy equipment and PQC extend across sectors. In a Certes survey of 200 IT and security professionals engaged with quantum-related risks at large US and UK organizations published in May, 78% of respondents rated the potential quantum threat to legacy environments as very high. For edge and IoT equipment, including industrial and medical devices, ATMs, and vehicles, 43% rated the threat as very high and another 31% as significant. Some devices will need alternative solutions Healthcare information, financial records, and trade secrets, such as code and industrial designs, can remain sensitive years after transmission. But not all data exchanged between devices has the same confidentiality requirements or operational relevance over time. “What’s missing from the policy conversation is a differentiated threat and risk assessment framework — one that accounts for data lifetime and sensitivity decay rate, device class, computational constraints, and realistic adversary capability timelines,” Sharon Hagi, CSO at IoT cybersecurity firm Finite State, told CSO in June after France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, outlined plans to introduce PQC requirements for product qualification starting in 2027. “The quantum threat is not uniformly distributed across the cryptographic stack,” Hagi said. “Shor’s algorithm breaks RSA and ECC. It does not break AES-256 or SHA-3 in any operationally practical sense — Grover’s provides at most a quadratic speedup, and the effective security margins of properly sized symmetric primitives still holds for most uses. Architectures that rely on symmetric encryption with out-of-band or pre-provisioned key distribution remain meaningful options for resource-constrained embedded devices where NIST PQC algorithms (e.g. ML-KEM, ML-DSA) impose non-trivial compute, bandwidth, and memory costs.” This means vendors will have to weigh carefully on which devices it’s even viable due to hardware limitations to deploy new PQC algorithms. In some cases, end-users might have to come up with alternatives, such as isolating those devices and routing traffic to and from them through other gateway devices that can apply PQC. This is the approach that users should start taking before vendors decide to release firmware upgrades, dos Santos says. For example, internet-facing websites and portals should already be configured to use TLS 1.3 as all modern browsers support it. For remote management and file transfers over the internet, deploy gateways that support protocols with quantum-resistant cryptography. A hospital could use a gateway to protect an image transfer to an external radiology provider. The hospital would still need to assess the connection from the scanner or image archive to that gateway and maybe isolate them on their own network segment with no direct internet access. “But at least for the external part, you’re reducing risk, right?” dos Santos says. But PQC support at one endpoint is effective only if the other endpoint can also negotiate the same algorithm, and manufacturers are reporting difficulty meeting interoperability goals. Thales’s September Manufacturing Data Threat Report , based on 417 respondents in 20 countries, revealed that 30% were behind on their post-quantum interoperability objectives. “For the end users, the main thing to be doing right now is the inventory of devices and data together,” dos Santos said. “Devices, data, and communication.” The resulting map should identify which transfers already have compatible protection, which depend on an upgrade, and where a gateway could protect an external connection. For healthcare, Forescout recommends prioritizing patient portals, external APIs, partner exchanges, and other internet-facing connections, then updating cryptographic libraries and firmware where feasible. For equipment that cannot be upgraded, its healthcare report recommends assessing gateways and isolation measures, obtaining vendor roadmaps, and planning replacement when manufacturers have no viable migration path. Dos Santos says vendors supplying equipment with multiyear service should have a roadmap for PQC communications even when their current firmware does not support it. Operators need to know when that support will arrive, which connections it will protect, and whether it requires new hardware. For equipment expected to remain in service for years, those answers need to inform purchasing and support agreements, alongside a replacement plan if a vendor cannot deliver an upgrade. The G7 call to action urges organizations to integrate quantum-safe replacements into normal equipment renewal schedules and the US Office of Management and Budget’s June guidance directs federal agencies to incorporate PQC upgrades into hardware refreshes and prioritize replacing or decommissioning equipment that cannot support PQC or hybrid cryptography.
summary: Quantum-resistant cryptography presents security leaders with various challenges, but CISOs in industries dependent on IoT and operational technology (OT) devices may face a particularly difficult journey to quantum readiness, especially if sensitive information that must remain confidential for years passes through those devices. A recent report from cybersecurity firm Forescout highlights these challenges in the healthcare industry, where medical histories, diagnostic images, and laboratory results, which retain their sensitivity long after they are created, routinely get transferred between various operational systems. Attackers who collect encrypted traffic carrying this information today can store it for decryption when sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available, an approach security experts call “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL). “PQC [post-quantum cryptography] migration in healthcare is not just about data confidentiality, but also patient safety,” the Forescout researchers say in their report, which examined over 2.5 million devices across more than 50 organizations.

title: F5 rushes out emergency NGINX patches for three critical flaws
raw_text: F5 is once again disclosing cybersecurity flaws in its core offerings. The app delivery and security provider has released out-of-band (OOB) security patches that address multiple flaws in NGINX, its high-performance software that controls digital traffic for websites. These include three critical-severity flaws that could allow attackers to crash systems, execute code, and launch denial of service (DoS) attacks. OOB security patches are emergency software updates released outside of normal maintenance cycles. CVE-2026-15176 , CVE-2026-97205 , and CVE-2026-93479 are rated 9.2 in severity in the latest version (4.0) of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Impacted software products include NGINX Plus, NGINX Open Source, NGINX Ingress Controller, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and NGINX Instance Manager. While F5 says it hasn’t discovered evidence that these issues are being exploited in the wild, it advises customers to install or upgrade to fixed versions. Analysts agree. “NGINX is the front door: Reverse proxy, load balancer, and Kubernetes ingress,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, noting that transport layer security (TLS) usually terminates in NGINX. “Code execution on that box means seeing passwords, session cookies, and API tokens in the clear, plus the private keys that make it all trustworthy.” Allowing attackers to crash systems CVE-2026-15176 and CVE-2026-97205 are ngx_http_core_module vulnerabilities in F5’s NGINX, which could cause a heap buffer overflow in the server’s worker process. This type of memory corruption could lead to a system crashing or restarting, thus giving attackers access. Threat actors could also execute code on systems where Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a technique intended to prevent exploitation by randomly arranging memory locations when an app starts, is disabled, or bypass ASLR altogether. The flaws could allow attackers to launch DoS attacks to make the server inaccessible to legitimate users, F5 explained. CVE-2026-93479 is similar, in that it is a map directive flaw that could allow attackers to send crafted HTTP requests to cause a heap buffer overflow; they can also execute code when ASLR is disabled, or bypass it. These vulnerabilities follow F5’s disclosure of CVE-2026-42530 in June. The flaw in ngx_http_v3_module in NGINX Open Source could also potentially allow remote attackers to cause DoS or trigger code execution. Customers can mitigate CVE-2026-15176 by avoiding use of the $request_filename variable and the alias directive in a location block, F5 said, and CVE-2026-97205 can be mitigated by disabling asynchronous file I/O (AIO) and Server Side Includes (SSI). Meanwhile, F5 advised mitigating CVE-2026-93479 by avoiding unnamed captures and instead using named captures and limiting their usage to the block with the regex match. But, noted Seva Ioussoufovitch , senior research analyst at Infotech, “since NGINX is used across a wide swath of systems, this may increase the risk of service availability loss for many enterprises.” The latest in a series of cybersecurity issues While these three vulnerabilities are not known to be exploited in the wild, F5 has repeatedly borne the brunt of cyberattacks in recent years, which is troubling because the cybersecurity and app delivery networking (ADN) company serves tens of thousands of customers, including 80% of the Fortune 500, analysts noted. Threat actors have repeatedly targeted flaws in its systems and products to map internal servers, hijack devices, breach systems, steal sensitive documents, and deploy data-wiping malware . Over the last five years, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged eight actively-exploited F5 vulnerabilities; four of these have been targeted in ransomware attacks . For instance, a 2025 nation-state breach and CISA’s Emergency Directive 26-01 centered on F5’s BIG-IP, and F5 said at the time that NGINX source code was not accessed. But, Dickson noted, NGINX’s own “warning shot” came in May when CVE-2026-42945 , a rewrite module overflow nicknamed NGINX Rift, arrived with a public remote code execution proof of concept. “This week’s alias and rewrite flaw lives in the same neighborhood,” he said, pointing out, “attackers read changelogs, too.” Mitigation Ioussoufovitch noted that the flaws are configuration-dependent, so enterprises should begin with an audit of current NGINX configurations to help risk-prioritize this patch. F5 also said that the risk of remote code execution (RCE) notably increases when ASLR is disabled, so users should double-check that ASLR and other typical OS-level protections are proactively enabled to at least limit the exploitation risk from similar types of attack. Enterprises need to ensure they have a clear inventory of which of their systems are running NGINX, including those where it is embedded in other products. This is critical to supporting configuration audits, segmentation efforts, and NGINX worker monitoring efforts, which can indicate that attackers “are poking at these types of vulnerabilities,” Ioussoufovitch said. “NGINX has already had multiple security releases this year, and I expect the trend to continue well into the future,” he noted. Dickson agreed that inventorying is the first step. NGINX “hides inside” ingress controllers, appliances, and container images. Many teams get NGINX from their Linux distribution, not nginx.org, and Amazon Linux still lists the AIO fix as pending. “A fix on the vendor’s site does not patch your servers,” he cautioned. As well as performing the inventory, enterprises should search their configurations for aliases paired with rewrite, AIO paired with SSI, and map blocks using unnamed regex captures. If an organization cannot patch today, the workarounds are simple, Dickson said: Disable AIO or stop serving SSI pages; switch map to named captures; confirm ASLR is on, run workers unprivileged; and segment the front door so it cannot reach the crown jewels. And, watch for worker processes that keep restarting. “These flaws need the right configuration to bite, and that is the good news,” Dickson said. “The bad news is that many organizations may not know what their NGINX configurations actually say.”

The app delivery and security provider has released out-of-band (OOB) security patches that address multiple flaws in NGINX, its high-performance software that controls digital traffic for websites. These include three critical-severity flaws that could allow attackers to crash systems, execute code, and launch denial of service (DoS) attacks. OOB security patches are emergency software updates released outside of normal maintenance cycles.

title: Microsoft, Nvidia push provenance checks as open-weight AI adoption accelerates
raw_text: Microsoft and Nvidia are urging enterprises to assess the security of open-weight AI models throughout deployment, warning that changes to model weights and configurations can weaken safeguards even when a model retains its ability to perform assigned tasks. In a joint paper published last week, the companies identified 30 risk types across five categories and outlined a process for evaluating, mitigating, and monitoring them. The guidance calls for enterprises to verify model provenance, test the configurations they intend to deploy, and reassess risks after material changes. “Weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk,” the paper said . “Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards.” The framework covers cybersecurity, data protection, content, human-AI interaction, and bias. Its cybersecurity category includes malicious code generation, malicious tool calls, extraction of the model’s safety policies, excessive token generation, and behavior that diverges from the intended system goal. The paper draws on existing NIST and ISO risk-management standards and is the first in a planned series on managing risks across open-weight AI deployments, the companies said in a blog post. Model changes can weaken safeguards Open-weight models can be fine-tuned, merged with other models, modified, or repackaged for different uses. But those changes can weaken a model’s safety protections even when it continues to perform its intended task well, Microsoft and Nvidia said. “Safety behaviors are often the more fragile of the two,” the companies wrote. Changes to model weights, fine-tuning, quantization and configuration can “degrade safeguards while leaving task performance intact.” That creates a challenge for enterprise security teams: a model may continue to deliver accurate results on routine tasks even after changes have affected how it responds to unsafe requests. The companies advise enterprises to assess safety and capability separately, test the specific model configuration they intend to deploy, and repeat evaluations after significant changes. “No volume of behavioral testing establishes what an artifact is, only how it behaves,” the paper said. It recommends using cryptographic signatures to verify that a model matches the publisher’s original artifact. “Where signatures are unavailable, record the unverified integrity as an open risk rather than treating evaluation results as closing it,” the paper recommended. For enterprises, Gartner recommends independent adversarial testing, static scanning of model files, and provenance verification before and after deployment. Gartner’s proposed vetting process also calls for verifying model sources, checking file integrity, conducting adversarial testing, and recording approved models in an enterprise registry. Security must extend beyond the model Microsoft and Nvidia caution that evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of the application built around it. “Model evaluation alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application; enterprises must also assess permissions, data access, connected tools, runtime behavior, and operational controls,” the paper says. The guidance recommends assessing models in their intended operating context and maintaining controls across the model, runtime, harness, and application layers. It also calls for monitoring model inputs, outputs, and tool use after deployment. According to Gartner, open-weight model traffic must be routed through governed AI gateways to enforce authentication, prompt-injection defenses, sensitive-data protection and audit logging. The research firm also recommends isolating self-hosted runtimes and applying controls suited to other deployment models, including private network paths and customer-managed encryption keys for cloud API consumption. Gartner reported that client inquiries about open-weight models through its research inquiry service rose by more than 30% in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the first quarter. The firm projects that open-weight models will account for 50% of enterprise AI use cases by 2028, up from 20% at the time of its report. Staffing and accountability matter Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said self-hosting requires enterprises to account for the people and processes needed to maintain safeguards. “Self-hosting is a staffing decision as much as an infrastructure one, and the people to carry it must move with the model,” Gogia said. He cautioned against assuming that self-hosting necessarily means replacing all the safeguards available through managed services. In his assessment, a significant gap can be the provider’s misuse-investigation function, while customer responsibilities depend on the service and its configuration. Gogia said the Microsoft-Nvidia paper provides useful guidance but leaves important areas for future work. The authors say subsequent publications will extend risk-management guidance across the runtime, harness, and application layers. “The sharper question is who is contractually obliged to re-test and patch the model when a new stripping technique lands,” Gogia said. For CISOs, Gogia recommends assessing the model, deployment, and intended use before approving production workloads. He also advises security teams to retain control of their risk registers rather than relying exclusively on a vendor-developed taxonomy.
summary: Microsoft and Nvidia are urging enterprises to assess the security of open-weight AI models throughout deployment, warning that changes to model weights and configurations can weaken safeguards even when a model retains its ability to perform assigned tasks. In a joint paper published last week, the companies identified 30 risk types across five categories and outlined a process for evaluating, mitigating, and monitoring them. The guidance calls for enterprises to verify model provenance, test the configurations they intend to deploy, and reassess risks after material changes. “Weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk,” the paper said .

title: ConnectWise backup credentials exposed multiple Microsoft 365 tenants
raw_text: ConnectWise has disabled key cloud services and is investigating unauthorized access to customers’ Microsoft 365 environments after a credential tied to its Cloud Backup platform was compromised and used to authenticate into customer tenants, prompting Huntress to identify suspicious sign-ins across 162 organizations. The activity involved the Cloud Backup application obtaining Microsoft Graph access tokens using a credential associated with ConnectWise’s own tenant. Security firm Huntress has also confirmed unauthorized sign-ins across 162 tenants as of 19:00 UTC on October 16. Huntress said the application authenticated from the IP address 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, between 06.13 and 08.34 UTC. The address belonged to a hosting provider, rather than the Azure private IP space from which the application normally communicated. The authentication events were recorded in Microsoft’s sign-in logs. ConnectWise has acknowledged the activity and has disabled seven application identities on October 17. It also suspended Cloud Backup, along with SaaS Security and Cloud Management. Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company updated its advisory on October 19 and said it had not observed successful threat activity in the environments it monitors since implementing containment measures, but had yet to establish a timeline for restoring the services. “Existing backup archives remain encrypted and isolated, and we have no indication that those archives have been compromised,” noted ConnectWise. The October 19 advisory update included two additional IP addresses, 144.172.64[.]99 and 144.172.64[.]60, identified through downstream security monitoring. Integration credentials used to escalate access ConnectWise Cloud Backup needs broad permissions to back up and restore customer data across Microsoft 365 services, including Exchange Online, OneDrive, SharePoint and Teams. Huntress said the compromised credential allowed the application to obtain Microsoft Graph tokens in customer tenants without requiring an individual user to sign in. That application-based authentication does not involve a user password or trigger the multi-factor authentication ( MFA ) prompt associated with a usual login. The credential lives in the vendor’s own environment, meaning customers could not have generated it through activity in their individual tenants. Huntress also identified activity involving a second ConnectWise application, Cloud Management for Microsoft Teams, in one partner tenant. According to the security firm, the application assigned itself the Global Administrator role and added credentials to two other applications, including a Huntress application specific to that partner. The sequence took approximately five minutes, Huntress said, adding that it had not established whether the separate stages of activity were conducted by the same operator. Service suspensions buy time, but tenant-level checks remain necessary ConnectWise disabled the seven application identities and revoked certificates associated with affected application connections. The company said those actions prevent new authentication through the disabled connections but do not automatically reverse changes already made inside customer tenants. Previously issued access tokens may also remain usable until they expire or are otherwise invalidated, it added. The service disruption extends beyond backups. With Cloud Backup suspended, scheduled backups, access to affected archives, and restoration capabilities remain unavailable. SaaS Security monitoring and alerting, as well as Cloud Management’s user and license management functions, have also been taken offline while remediation continues. Huntress said its investigation had not confirmed data theft. In the one tenant whose audit logs it examined in detail, the firm found no recorded mail or file access, but warned that this did not prove that no data had been taken. Some Microsoft Graph directory reads do not leave an audit trail, limiting what investigators can establish from available records, it noted. Both companies have urged partners and customer administrators to review their Microsoft 365 environments. ConnectWise’s guidance calls for checks of application sign-ins, credentials, directory roles, consent grants, policy changes, and possible mailbox forwarding or other persistence mechanisms. ConnectWise partners were also advised to keep affected applications disabled until it provides formal restoration instructions. As of October 19, investigation and service restoration efforts remained ongoing.

The activity involved the Cloud Backup application obtaining Microsoft Graph access tokens using a credential associated with ConnectWise’s own tenant. Security firm Huntress has also confirmed unauthorized sign-ins across 162 tenants as of 19:00 UTC on October 16. Huntress said the application authenticated from the IP address 144.172.64[.]128 on October 15, between 06.13 and 08.34 UTC.

title: The password nobody owns: Taking machines to zero standing privilege (ZSP)
raw_text: Ask your infrastructure lead who owns the service account behind the overnight finance batch and notice how long the answer takes. In many of the environments I’ve reviewed, the engineer who set it up left years ago and the password has been sitting in a vault, or sometimes a plain config file, ever since. It usually still carries permissions sized for a migration that wrapped up before anyone on the current team joined, so people leave it alone rather than risk breaking something nobody fully understands. Multiply that across the landscape, and the numbers get uncomfortable quickly. Palo Alto Networks surveyed more than 2,900 security leaders for its 2026 Identity Security Landscape and found an average of 109 machine identities for every human one. I’d treat any single ratio with some caution, since each vendor counts identities differently. The same report’s finding that 61% of privileged access requests are still met with standing privilege, instead of being granted on demand, is much harder to wave away. Entro Labs looked at the age of these identities too. Close to half were more than a year old, and 7.5% had been around for somewhere between five and ten years. Over the past decade, most security programmes have put real effort into controlling human admins through PAM. Machine accounts tended to get a vault and a rotation schedule, and in most of the programmes I’ve worked on, that’s roughly where the effort on them ended. Why rotation only buys you time Vaulting and rotating a service account password beats leaving it hard-coded in a script, and I wouldn’t advise anyone to pull out a vault that’s working. Rotation changes the secret, though it leaves the access exactly as it was. Between one change and the next, the credential stays valid with every permission intact, readable from wherever the application fetches it. If an attacker copies it a few days into a ninety-day cycle, they’ve got close to three months to use it quietly. OAuth integrations make this worse, because a refresh token can keep renewing itself long after anyone remembers granting it. The Salesloft Drift campaign in August 2025 is the clearest recent example I can point to. Google Threat Intelligence Group reported that the actor it tracks as UNC6395 used stolen OAuth and refresh tokens tied to the Drift integration to pull data out of Salesforce customer instances between 8 and 18 August, and more than 700 organisations were caught up in it. Because the tokens were genuine and no person was signing in, there was no MFA prompt to trip and nothing unusual for the authentication layer to notice. I suspect plenty of the affected customers would have struggled to name who in their own team had approved that integration in the first place. I’d want every CIO to look closely at what the attackers were after. Customers were told to search their Salesforce records for secrets such as AWS keys and Snowflake tokens, since support cases are a common place for staff to paste credentials while troubleshooting. In other words, the stolen standing token was being used to hunt for more standing tokens in other systems. Salesloft later linked the initial access to a compromise of its GitHub account back in March, months before the theft began. width="1024" height="469" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1024px) 100vw, 1024px"> Figure 1: Standing credential vs zero standing privilege . Ashish Mishra What zero standing privilege looks like for a machine With zero standing privilege, a machine identity holds no usable access while it sits idle. When it has work to do, it proves who it is to a policy engine and gets back a short-lived credential scoped to that job, which expires on its own once the job finishes. Most of you will already have something like this for people, usually as just-in-time elevation through a PAM platform. Workloads tend to get there through workload identity federation instead. The workload presents a signed token from a platform the target already trusts, such as a Kubernetes cluster or a CI pipeline, and swaps it for temporary access. GitHub Actions deploying into AWS is the easiest case to picture. The pipeline requests an OIDC token from GitHub, AWS checks it against a trust policy tied to that repository, and the job runs under a role whose credentials last around an hour by default. No access key gets stored in the repo at any point. Google’s own authentication action for GitHub recommends federation over exported service account keys on the same grounds, warning that those keys are long-lived and need the same care as a password. Getting there without breaking production Full zero standing privilege across every machine identity isn’t achievable in most enterprises right now, and it’s worth saying so plainly to your board. Older applications that log in to a database with a username and password won’t federate, and plenty of vendor appliances only accept a static API key. Practitioners increasingly describe near-zero standing privilege as the realistic target for machines, which is how I’d frame it too. Everything starts with an inventory. You need every machine credential in one place, including the OAuth grants your SaaS integrations hold, with a named human owner recorded against each. The owner field can look like admin overhead, but an account with no owner tends to survive every clean-up exercise, because nobody has the authority to approve switching it off. Once the list exists, sort it by what an attacker could reach with each credential. CI/CD pipelines and cloud admin roles usually end up near the top, and they also happen to be where federation is most mature, so moving pipelines to OIDC tends to be one of the earliest wins. Connected SaaS apps deserve a separate look. A lot of them were approved years ago with broad scopes, often by a business team rather than security, and nobody has revisited them since. Cut the scopes down to what each integration actually uses. It’s also fair to ask suppliers how they store the refresh tokens they hold on your behalf, and after Drift, a vendor with access to your CRM should have a ready answer. Some systems won’t federate for years. In those cases, you can still shorten how long a credential lives, even if you can’t change what it’s allowed to do. Vault-issued dynamic secrets work well here, with the database account created when the session starts and dropped when it closes, and the application usually needs little or no rewriting. For board reporting, the number I’d track is the share of machine access granted on demand compared with the share held permanently. Expect the first reading to look poor. It’s still worth putting in front of the board early, since the change from one quarter to the next tells them far more about progress than any single snapshot.
summary: Ask your infrastructure lead who owns the service account behind the overnight finance batch and notice how long the answer takes. In many of the environments I’ve reviewed, the engineer who set it up left years ago and the password has been sitting in a vault, or sometimes a plain config file, ever since. It usually still carries permissions sized for a migration that wrapped up before anyone on the current team joined, so people leave it alone rather than risk breaking something nobody fully understands. Multiply that across the landscape, and the numbers get uncomfortable quickly.

title: 9 rising malware trends every security pro should know
raw_text: Malware is evolving rapidly, driven by advances in AI and changes in computing infrastructures. Security professionals must continuously educate themselves on these trends to defend against increasingly sophisticated threats. The traditional game of cat and mouse between security attackers and defenders has got fiercer with fresh techniques evolving and older less effective approaches falling out of fashion. Here is a look at what’s heating up in the world of malware — and what’s cooling off. Infostealers commoditizing initial access Infostealers have experienced huge growth in the past 18 months, with malware such as Lumma Stealer , StealC, and RisePro now responsible for 75% of all stolen credentials, according to cybersecurity vendor Immersive. Infostealers steal browser cookies, VPN credentials, multi-factor authentication (MFA) tokens, crypto wallet data, and more. Cybercriminals sell the data that infostealers grab through dark web markets , giving attackers easy access to corporate systems. “This shift commoditizes initial access, enabling nation-state goals through simple transactions rather than complex attacks,” says Ben McCarthy, lead cyber security engineer at Immersive. Malicious packages targeting developer environments Threat actors are systematically compromising the software supply chain by embedding malicious code within legitimate development tools, libraries, and frameworks that organizations use to build applications. “These supply chain attacks exploit the trust between developers and package repositories,” Immersive’s McCarthy tells CSO. “Malicious packages often mimic legitimate ones while running harmful code, evading standard code reviews.” Popular software development ecosystems such as NPM , PyPI , and AI platforms like HuggingFace are frequent targets of malicious actors seeking to seed compromised packages in software developers’ toolchains. Attackers continued to innovate in 2026 when targeting the software supply chain as a vector for malware delivery. For example, the Shai-Hulud attacks involved self-propagating malware that stole CI/CD secrets and hijacked GitHub Actions OIDC tokens to publish malicious package versions through victims’ own release pipelines. Similar tactics were in play in other attacks. “In the Axios compromise , attackers targeted the lead maintainer’s credentials and inserted a malicious dependency into legitimate software releases,” says Lindsey O’Donnell-Welch, principal technical writer at managed detection and response firm Huntress. “This led to downstream dependencies downloading remote-access malware tailored to the operating system.” Ransomware becoming more targeted and sophisticated The ransomware landscape shifted dramatically after law enforcement cracked down on major groups like LockBit. Modern ransomware threat actors such as RansomHub and Akira now favor smaller, highly targeted attacks, using ransomware as a final step after full infiltration and data exfiltration. This marks a move from broad, opportunistic strikes to focused, high-value campaigns. “These targeted approaches show threat actors’ growing insight into specific vulnerabilities and their readiness to invest heavily in reconnaissance and tailored attack development,” Immersive’s McCarthy comments. These groups use advanced evasion techniques such as living-off-the-land (LOTL) tactics and legitimate admin tools to stay hidden. They’re also shifting from file encryption to data theft and extortion, threatening public leaks to pressure victims. “There’s been a notable uptick in the use of cloud-based services and remote management platforms as part of ransomware toolchains,” says Jamie Moles, senior technical marketing manager at network detection and response provider ExtraHop. “This aligns with a broader trend: Rather than relying solely on traditional malware payloads, adversaries are increasingly shifting toward abusing trusted platforms and ‘living-off-the-land’ techniques.” Healthcare remains a top target of ransomware attacks , while critical infrastructure faces increasing threats as attackers exploit the urgency that prompts quick ransom payments. Malware adopting social engineering techniques Cybercriminals are increasingly adopting ClickFix as a malware delivery method in attacks that rely on social engineering techniques to successfully infect end-user devices. ClickFix tricks users into executing malicious code — usually a PowerShell script — on their own systems, taking advantage of growing user fatigue in having to jump through online hoops to ‘prove you’re human.’ By hijacking trust in familiar CAPTCHA processes, threat actors are getting users to actively participate in their own compromise — copying and pasting malicious commands into their systems under the guise of simple verification. “We’ve seen this technique gain serious traction across phishing sites, compromised webpages, and social engineering campaigns,” says Jim Walter, senior threat researcher at SentinelLABS. “It’s simple, effective, and increasingly common.” CISOs need to be wary of the threat because it bypasses many traditional detection methods by relying on human behavior rather than system vulnerabilities. “Raising awareness, hardening endpoint execution policies, and deploying behavioral detection tools are essential to countering this wave of malware delivery,” Walter advises. Threat actors continue to bring new flavors of ClickFix into play in 2026. For example, Huntress logged a ClickFix lure in April dressed up as a free image-editing tool, which then led to a loader called CastleLoader before the attack chain dropped NetSupport RAT and a custom .NET stealer. “The end goal was to steal browser credentials, wallet extension data, and Telegram session files,” according to Huntress’ O’Donnell-Welch. Polymorphic malware evading detection mechanisms Polymorphic malware automatically modifies its code each time it replicates or infects a new system, making it difficult for signature-based detection methods to identify it. This type of malware is challenging for antivirus software to detect and for security researchers to analyze. Alex Hinchliffe, principal threat researcher at Unit 42, the threat intelligence and incident response arm at Palo Alto Networks, says, “Very basic or specific detection mechanisms, such as hash-based scanners, are thwarted by polymorphism, but it’s worth noting that each time a malicious program is compiled — e.g., into an executable — it will yield a new unique fingerprint or hash. Add to this the plethora of free and commercially available compressor, packer, and protector tools, which can be applied to a compiled program, and the ‘same’ program will yield yet more variations and permutations of the same fingerprint.” Polymorphic malware also often uses encryption to hide its payload, further complicating detection and analysis. AI ‘flattening’ the once diverse malware development ecosystem The malware ecosystem is consolidating and shrinking partly due to greater use of AI. “There isn’t much of a necessity anymore for exploit kit developers, loaders, and feature-rich malware implants,” says Adam Brown, principal threat intelligence analyst at Huntress. What once was a diverse and federated ecosystem of malware developers and service providers has been “flattened with the introduction of AI, and the business efficiency of smash-and-grab intrusion techniques”, Brown says. Threat actors frequently use trial accounts for their tooling (e.g., ScreenConnect) and cover their command and control (C2) and exfiltration routes under Cloudflare accounts. “Free-cloud hosting is ubiquitous, negating the need and cost of bullet-proof hosters,” Brown adds. “As long as defenses are disabled prior, free and commercial toolsets — Cobalt Strike, Meterpreter, Bloodhound, et al — work just as well.” In addition, cybercriminal syndicates are increasingly forgoing investment in and development of fully featured trojans, exploit kits, and even dedicated hosting as part of a ruthless business-like optimization of cybercrime activity. “It is far more efficient for them [cybercrime syndicates] to disable defenses using legitimate executables — signed system drivers, remote management software, etc. — deploy easily coded info-stealers, leverage legitimate and ubiquitous tooling to laterally move, and execute a network-wide encryption of enterprise assets,” Brown explains. AI is speeding up existing attacks Although AI is yet to displace traditional attack methods, a range of security vendors report that attackers are using AI to make existing techniques faster and more convincing, while also allowing them to operate at greater scale. “It [AI] can help write phishing messages and automate reconnaissance, while also supporting faster vulnerability discovery and more realistic impersonation attempts,” says Patricia Leppert, team manager of customer trust and security at TeamViewer. But attackers are also using AI to build malware and related tooling. eSentire Threat Research Unit reports logging signs of AI-assisted development by attackers ranging from ransomware affiliates to a North Korean cyberespionage group. “Attackers use large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek to write loaders, droppers, admin panels and scripts, to convert code between languages, and to write social-engineering text,” says Spence Hutchinson, senior manager of intelligence research at eSentire. “They get past the models’ safeguards through jailbreaking, or through stolen and resold accounts.” Attackers adopting modern development techniques Malware developers are also using modern software development practices. For example, security vendor Barracuda reports a growing use of modern programming languages such as Rust and Go in malware, especially ransomware binaries. “These languages allow developers to build malware that is more portable and easier to adapt across operating systems,” explains Christine Barry, senior chief cybersecurity storyteller and content manager for the office of the CTO at Barracuda. “Rather than maintaining separate malware families for Windows, Linux, and virtualization environments, threat actors can support multiple platforms from a common code base.” Agentic AI enters the fray Attackers are already using generative AI to create phishing emails, write malicious code, and accelerate social-engineering attacks. But agentic AI will push their capabilities further by combining LLMs with tools, memory, and decision-making capabilities that enable a malicious system to plan actions, adapt to obstacles, and pursue objectives autonomously. JadePuffer offers a recent example of such an agentic AI attack. “This attack conducted reconnaissance, adapted to changing conditions, harvested credentials, moved through the target environment, and carried out destructive actions with limited evidence of human interaction or control,” Barracuda’s Barry says. “Researchers also observed JadePuffer modifying its behavior when it encountered problems, allowing the attack to adapt to conditions that might interrupt a scripted attack.” Depreciated malware techniques Some noticeable trends reflect a “downturn” for malware and hacking techniques that have fallen out of fashion, mainly because their effectiveness has decreased due to advances in security defenses. For example, threat actors rely more on legitimate admin tools — such as Sysinternals Suite and living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) — for evasion and persistence, and less on malicious executables. “On the hacking tool front, we observed a decrease in the use of more comprehensive tool suites like Cobalt Strike and Sliver,” says O’Donnell-Welch of Huntress. “However, threat actors continue to use specialized tools like Mimikatz and CrackMapExec for functionalities like password sniffing, memory dumping, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.” Other once popular techniques that have fallen out of favor include: Network worms , such as Conficker, because modern networks now feature segmentation, automated patching, and strong endpoint defenses, all of which limit worm propagation Traditional botnets Exploit kits , which were once a prevalent method for delivering malware through web-based attacks by scanning users’ systems for known vulnerabilities in software such as Adobe Flash, Java, or Internet Explorer, and then exploiting those weaknesses to install malware Office macros USB-based malware

title: Google Cloud power event knocks out UK banks, courts and couriers
raw_text:
A power problem in Google Cloud’s London region knocked out banking apps, the courts’ video platform and delivery networks across the UK on Tuesday 20 October, with no second Google UK region for customers to fall back on.

By late afternoon, most services had recovered. Google said the issue affected only a “very small number” of customers, while the Ministry of Justice confirmed the courts’ Cloud Video Platform had still not fully recovered. Google said: “We will publish an analysis of this incident once we have completed our internal investigation.”

The outage began just after 7.00am BST when the europe-west2-b availability zone – one of three inside Google’s London region, europe-west2 – lost power. Google Cloud confirmed the cause: “A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. We are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritising the recovery of existing workloads.”

The incident is the latest reminder that the UK’s largest businesses remain dangerously exposed to cloud outages. Because europe-west2 is Google’s only UK region, customers that had not built multi-region resilience had no second UK location to failover to.

The failure hit four Google Cloud locations:

  1. europe-west2 (London) – Google’s only UK region, where the failure struck.
  2. europe-west2-b – the availability zone that lost power.
  3. europe-west2-a and europe-west2-c – the peer zones that, by one engineer’s account, did not fully absorb the load.
  4. europe-north2 – one administrator also reported VPC, Cloud NAT and load-balancer issues here.

For UK customers, the outage rippled through a long list of household names:

  • Banks and fintech: Revolut, Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Barclays, Bank of Scotland, NatWest, Halifax, Nationwide, Emma and credit-reference firm Equifax.
  • Delivery and retail: Royal Mail, DPD and Screwfix.
  • Property and web services: Rightmove, BT and hosting firm SiteGround.
  • Public sector: NHS England, HM Courts & Tribunals Service and Gov.uk.

The day unfolded like this:

  • 07.05 – VPC, Cloud NAT and load-balancer issues began in europe-west2, with one administrator also reporting europe-north2.
  • 10.00 – The courts’ Cloud Video Platform went down across large parts of England and Wales.
  • 10.57 – Google confirmed “an issue with multiple services in europe-west2”.

  • 11.16 – NHS England, HM Courts & Tribunals Service and Gov.uk appeared to be affected.
  • 11.27 – The Criminal Bar Association warned that trials and hearings “can not proceed”.
  • 12.27 – Google said the power event was mitigated and partial mitigation would follow within 30 minutes.
  • 12.45 – The first administrators reported virtual machines in europe-west2-b rebooted and services restored.
  • 14.48 – Google reported “recovery of services for most workloads in europe-west2”.

  • 15.52 – The Ministry of Justice confirmed its systems were not yet fully restored.

The failure also played out in real time on Reddit among the IT professionals who had to manage it. One engineer posting as Rs3_Myway, who said they were “on calls at work dealing with it”, wrote: “Availability zone B went down with power cut. A and C, for some reason, didn’t pick up the slack completely in prod (unclear why). Apigee gateway as the big problem system.”

An administrator relaying Google’s engineering update described the root cause: “Although mains power has returned, backup generators failed to engage during the initial outage. As a result, Engineering is maintaining a frontend and backend drain on the europe-west2-b clusters while onsite technicians verify backend power functionality.”

Another user summed up the structural problem: “It is the only Google region in the UK so businesses/banks/NHS etc. here can’t switch to another location.”

And an IT manager posting as Crimsondelo reported the fallout across their own supply chain: “We are seeing outages on several of our providers including Equifax. Apparently Lloyds is having issues as well.”

The episode echoes an Amazon Web Services outage that knocked out UK tax office and banking services last autumn, and it lands as investment banks lose £600,000 an hour to IT failures. For enterprise buyers, the lesson is architectural – a single-zone service in a single-region footprint remains a single point of failure, and data sovereignty does little to help when the only region available is the one that went down.
