title: AstraZeneca works with Oracle to speed up drug trials
raw_text:
AstraZeneca is working with Oracle to investigate the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and real-world data to help identify eligible patients for clinical trials. The two companies also plan to accelerate evidence generation, and bring relevant research insights into everyday care using Oracle’s health data, cloud, AI, analytics and clinical workflow capabilities.

Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca CEO, described the collaboration as “unique”. “Combining AstraZeneca’s world-class science with Oracle’s deep data and technology expertise, we can help clinicians identify patients sooner, optimise clinical trials, and generate evidence continuously across the lifecycle of a medicine,” he said.

Anne-Claire Gerbaldi, chief digital, data and AI officer at AstraZeneca, said the use of AI to improve clinical trials is the next evolution of medicine. “Too many patients are diagnosed late or face a long journey to get the care they need,” she said. “To build the next decade of medicine, we aim to harness AI to connect learnings across science, clinical trials and everyday care, generating insights that continuously strengthen research, accelerate innovation and enhance patient outcomes.”

Through a non-binding agreement, the companies plan to explore selected use cases that could improve clinical trial efficiency and success by leveraging modern applications and AI to help care teams identify eligible patients earlier and easier, resulting in greater access to clinical trials for patients in need and helping to overcome one of the largest obstacles in clinical trials – patient recruitment. Disease areas the two companies are looking to explore include oncology; cardiovascular, renal and metabolic diseases; respiratory and immunology; and rare disease.

The collaboration is international and involves working with governments. Oracle and AstraZeneca plan to start with a focus on supporting hypertension care and clinical research in Abu Dhabi, in partnership with healthcare company M42. According to AstraZeneca, this will help clinical teams identify patients with uncontrolled hypertension; implementing guideline-directed care; and improving the recruitment for clinical trials.

“Some of the most important opportunities for AI are in healthcare, where better use of data can help turn scientific innovation into better outcomes for patients,” said Mike Sicilia, Oracle CEO.

“By bringing AstraZeneca’s scientific expertise together with Oracle’s data, cloud, AI and healthcare capabilities, we have an opportunity to help accelerate research, connect more patients to clinical trials, and ultimately bring relevant insights into care faster.”

title: FCA gets hundreds of applicants for two top artificial intelligence roles
raw_text:
The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has received hundreds of applications for two senior roles specialising in artificial intelligence (AI) and data science.

The advertised roles are for a head of agentic AI and data science research and a head of department, with salaries of between £126,000 and £190,000 per year.

According to a Bloomberg report, Jessica Rusu, the FCA’s chief information and AI officer, confirmed it has received hundreds of applicants for the two jobs.

She told Bloomberg: “We have two senior leadership roles in the market now and we have had hundreds of really high-quality applications.”

Both roles are now closed to applications.

Passion for AI and doing the right thing

One senior banking IT professional, who wished to remain anonymous, said the people applying for these jobs are in it for the “mission” rather than the money, which he said is less than they could earn in the private sector.

“I think these jobs appeal to people who truly are passionate about what happens to AI, regardless of what they get paid. I think there would be a queue of people who are not so worried about the pay,” he added. “They’re more interested in getting AI under control and getting it regulated and keeping a close eye on it.”

In July, a “landmark review” by the FCA described AI as a “defining force” that will change financial services for consumers, but one that could “amplify risks”.

The regulator’s push for the right advanced tech skills to help it combat increased tech-based threats and use tech to better regulate has been going on for half a decade.

FCA CEO Nikhil Rathi said last year that the regulator had “embraced data and technology to crack down on harm and ensure high standards”.

Building data and AI expertise

In 2022, as part of a “heavy” investment in data, the FCA said it wanted to hire people with expertise in AI, analytics and data science, as well as cloud engineering and digital technology. This was in addition to the 100 people it had hired since 2020.

At the time, Rusu said: “Better use of data means we can be more proactive and find and stop harm faster. We are continuing to improve our data, technology and capabilities to act decisively in consumers’ interests, while making it easier for firms to report to us.” 

It opened a new digital delivery centre in Leeds that year, and announced plans to double the number of staff in its Edinburgh office to around 200 and increase recruitment in data and technology. 

Rusu told a Bloomberg event in London that the FCA is building AI tools to help oversee anti-money laundering controls at 60,000 extra firms to meet new rules that come in 2028. She said it is also using AI agents to help supervise thousands of small firms that report wholesale market transactions.

Beyond using AI to regulate, the FCA wants to firm up defences against cyber security risks and potential fraud emanating from the technology.

“AI is moving faster than any regulatory framework was designed,” said Rusu. “That means regulators will increasingly need to make judgements without precedent, while ensuring that trust remains at the heart of financial services.”

title: Teachers’ pension transfers from Capita on eve of government’s civil service scheme decision
raw_text:
The switchover of the teachers’ pension scheme from Capita to Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), which begins this week, will be closely watched as government faces decision time over Capita’s failed civil service pension administration.

If all goes to plan, a blackout on the teachers’ pension website is planned from 22 October to 2 November, when the scheme completes its transfer to Indian IT giant TCS.

Capita has run the service for more than 20 years, but TCS secured a 10-year Department for Education contract in 2023, the same year Capita won the contract to take over the civil service pension scheme (CSPS), which since its go live has been a monumental disaster (see box below).

It won’t just be teachers braced for the transfer of more than two million pension accounts from Capita to TCS, but also the government, which is under pressure to strip Capita of the CSPS. It has already removed the outsourcing firm from the contract to administer the Royal Mail pension scheme, following failure to meet key milestones, and is still to decide the scheme’s future administration delivery.

Pension problems

As Computer Weekly revealed earlier this month, MPs heard that some teachers are experiencing problems with their pensions. In light of Capita’s disastrous takeover of the Civil Service Pension Scheme, a Westminster Hall debate was held, where MPs discussed the botched scheme.

During the packed-out meeting, Alison Bennet, Liberal Democrat MP for Mid Sussex, said she had been told teachers were experiencing problems with their pensions. She asked: “Are we seeing teachers go through the same ordeal [as civil servants]?

“I have received very concerning casework from teachers in my constituency who seem to be having similar or the same troubles with their pensions,” added Bennet. “The idea that the immense stress and potential financial hardship we’ve heard inflicted on civil servants has been [repeated] with teachers is appalling.”

One former teacher who is supporting teachers with concerns told Computer Weekly earlier this month that there are thousands of anomalies in the data being transferred that could see teachers lose out. “I have been encouraging teachers to make copies of the data that they have available through the website,” he said.

A Department for Education spokesperson repeated an earlier statement that the scheme has some “clearly unacceptable” delays. The spokesperson said it expects Capita to “closely with those affected … resolve issues as quickly as possible and keep them informed throughout”.

The government department confirmed the transfer will be complete on 1 November, with the website and member/employer portal available from 2 November.

TCS and Capita were contacted for an update on progress but had not responded when this article was published.

Decision time

The government is currently deciding what to do with the CSPS and Royal Mail schemes. It’s Strategic Review of Pension Scheme Delivery is at its “discovery phase”, where it is considering a range of options, including insourcing and increased digital delivery for the schemes.

In a recent briefing to members, PCS general secretary Fran Heathcote said the government hopes to develop its “strategic position” by next month. A decision, if made next month, will come soon after TCS’s teachers’ pension administration goes live.

Heathcote told union members that the government is considering the “feasibility of insourcing pension administration”, as well as “greater consistency and alignment across public service schemes, shared delivery approaches between schemes, future digital delivery options, and the practical implications of major organisational change”.

The PCS’s Heathcote also said the National Trade Union Congress has highlighted government ambitions to strengthen internal digital capability and said the review should examine: “The feasibility of an in-house digital pension platform. The timescales required to develop such a system. Alternative suppliers if an internal solution is not viable.”

TCS’s takeover of the teachers’ pension scheme, which involves digitally transforming it, will give the government a live case to watch closely.

Botched AI project

Capita had planned a similar transformation with the CSPS but its grand plan to use artificial intelligence (AI) to revolutionise pension scheme delivery failed when the tech didn’t work.

Simon Hoare MP, who chairs the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee, said during a select committee hearing about the CSPS failures: “The Cabinet Office was told that the two-year transition period would lead to the digital artificial intelligence revolution to deliver a world-class, world-leading pension service. None of that met neither the novel nor the basic.”

Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez conceded: “We have not been able to deploy the technology that would allow us to get there.”

What resulted is becoming a scandal as retired civil servants and the families of deceased scheme members have been left without the funds they are owed – for nearly a year in some cases – due to Capta’s mistakes.

title: CIOs admit they are being forced to upgrade enterprise IT
raw_text:
A Censuswide survey of 2,018 CIOs and senior IT decision-makers at large organisations in the US and UK for independent software maintenance provider Origina has found that organisations spend almost $13m on upgrades pushed by IT providers.

On average, 28% of enterprise software budgets go on upgrades, migrations and licensing changes driven by their IT suppliers. IT leaders who took part in the study reported that their organisation would not have actively chosen to upgrade.

This has a profound effect on new projects, which extends to artificial intelligence (AI) initiatives. Asked about the last time an AI or data programme was slowed, paused or cancelled, 34% said IT supplier-driven costs made a major contribution to that decision, and a further 56% a moderate one.

The research published in Origina’s The software tax report, in partnership with Thinkers50, suggests these costs have shifted the balance of power between buyers and sellers. Customers exercise choice once, at the point of purchase. After that, control over the timing and terms of change passes largely to the IT supplier.

Out of those surveyed, 78% agree their primary provider of enterprise software, rather than their own organisation, sets the timing and terms of change. A similar proportion said they would have no meaningful choice but to accept if a major enterprise IT provider changed its commercial terms. Some 76% said their organisation has very little real leverage in negotiations, and 80% said moving away from major IT suppliers would cause significant disruption.

While software as a service (SaaS) and cloud computing make deployment, updates, access and security simpler, the report’s authors said that the shift from owning software to renting access also changed the economic relationship.

“Switching off a service became easier technically; switching away from the provider could become harder commercially and operationally,” they warned. “Over several decades, dependence accumulated with few external guardrails to constrain it.”

Marshall Van Alstyne, professor at Boston University and co-author of The software tax, said: “Economists have studied this problem for decades: once a customer makes relationship-specific investments, the vendor gains leverage that no contract can fully anticipate.

“For CIOs, the lesson is simple: negotiate the exit before the entry. You don’t have to leave a vendor to benefit from being able to.”

The report points out that an organisation can rationally accept an unfavourable upgrade if refusing it means losing support, creating a security risk or jeopardising access to software on which critical operations depend.

“What looks irrational when the upgrade is considered in isolation may be perfectly rational when the available alternatives are considered alongside it,” the report’s authors said. “The customers in this survey had a choice, but by the time it had to be made, their realistic options had already narrowed.”

Tomás O’Leary, CEO and founder of Origina and co-author of The Software Tax, said: “When the alternative to an unwanted upgrade is losing support on systems the business runs on, saying yes is often a rational response.

“That’s exactly the problem. The market has left some of the most experienced technology leaders in the world with little room to refuse, and that cost shows up in budgets, in engineering time and in innovation that never gets funded. We want to make that cost visible so customers can start to take back control of it.”

title: Keep less, know more: the AI advantage hiding in your data estate
raw_text:
Most organisations are preparing for AI by consolidating and retaining more data. But the stronger strategy is arguably the opposite. One of the most valuable ways to prepare for enterprise AI this year is actually to dispose of data. This runs counter to a decade of data strategy built around consolidation and the assumption that more data automatically delivers better outcomes. But doing a bit of housekeeping is, in fact, a fast route to a more effective AI roll-out and more defensible General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) position.

The estate your assistant will actually read

Data estates drift by accident rather than by design. Consider the SharePoint site a team set up in 2019 so an external contractor could reach a single document, which no one ever decommissioned. Or the four iterations of the expenses policy living on a server, three of them superseded, but none marked accordingly. Think of the shared drive left behind after a restructure that still contains a redundancy list, or an absence spreadsheet a former employee saved outside the HR system. The data had been protected simply because it was hard to find, although this was never an intentional security measure.

If you deploy an AI assistant that indexes everything on your systems, problems will inevitably arise at go-live. Personal data that should have been disposed of becomes trivially discoverable. When an AI assistant is presented with four versions of a policy and no indication of which is the most current, it is likely to answer from the wrong one with complete confidence.

Data minimisation, complimented by other key controls like role-based access control (RBAC), remain essential to ensure systems can only access information appropriate to a user's role and authority.

This isn’t just an IT headache, but a direct tax on AI efficacy, as the cost of inaction will hit performance. Gartner predicts that organisations that prioritise semantics in AI-ready data will increase their GenAI model accuracy by up to 80% and reduce costs by up to 60% by 2027, which shows the value of investment.

Dispose before you index

Most programmes plan to tackle these issues after the pilot phase. After all, few leaders are willing to fund a data clear-out for a capability that has yet to prove its value. However, the economics point the other way. A file deleted before it’s indexed is gone with just one click, whereas deleting it afterwards means removing it from the source repository, search indexes, cached embeddings, and potentially a model that will need retraining.

Sequencing therefore matters more than just the tooling. To fix this, it’s important to start looking at the data repositories that have no clear owner, which carry the highest ratio of risk to value, and apply a straightforward test to everything else. For example, if a document were quoted verbatim in a response to an employee next week, would that be acceptable? If the answer is no, it does not belong in scope, regardless of its speculative future value.

Ownership is the control most programmes lack

It’s always worth remembering that data becomes risky at the point that it becomes nobody’s responsibility. An employee leaves, their files remain, and often no one can say with confidence what they contain, whether they're still needed or whether they can be deleted. If you multiply that across a decade of turnover, it accounts for much of the exposure in most large organisations.

The answer is straightforward: every significant data set should have a named owner with the authority to make decisions about it. Not a committee or a lengthy approval process, but a person who can quickly decide whether an AI tool should have access to their part of the business. The most common cause of delay in AI approvals is not risk appetite, but the inability to establish who decides. Stripping away dead data and establishing this clear ownership is the exact mechanism that allows organisations to deploy AI further and faster than competitors bogged down in uncurated data swamps.

Purpose has to travel with the data

Purpose limitation is another area where these programmes often come unstuck. Information collected for one reason, such as payroll, can quietly become reference material for an assistant, simply because integration was easy. The safeguard is to attach purpose and lawful basis to the data itself, rather than burying them in a register that quickly falls out of date. Done properly, teams can see at a glance which datasets are suitable for a particular AI use case and which are not.

The instinct to consolidate everything into one repository deserves scrutiny. The European Data Protection Board’s draft guidelines on anonymisation, published in July, are clear that data stripped of identifiers remains personal data where it sits in a store that cannot be cleanly separated from records identifying individuals. Purpose-bound collections are easier to defend and easier to evaluate for accuracy.

  • Javvad Malik, KnowBe4: When the intern has admin rights: GDPR in the agentic age.
  • Haris Pylarinos, Hack The Box: GDPR wasn't designed for AI and that's a security problem.

Provenance, and the expiry of assurance

Responding properly to an access or erasure request also means knowing where each record originated and which downstream copies exist. Teams have long treated provenance as an engineering refinement that can be addressed later. But it is often the difference between a response measured in hours and one measured in months. The risk is that you tell someone their data has gone, confirm it to the individual, and leave the assistant answering from a copy nobody tracked.

Assurance ages the same way. An impact assessment signed in March describes a system that by September carries a different model version, new data sources and an agent performing actions nobody reviewed. It’s important to give assessments review dates and version references, so the evidence describes the up-to-date system in production.

Restraint as competitive advantage

There is time to do this deliberately. The Digital Omnibus has moved the AI Act’s obligations for higher risk standalone systems to December 2027, and the ICO has confirmed a statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision making for 2026 and 2027. That interval creates value only if it is spent on the estate rather than on documentation about it.

The organisations that get furthest with AI will not be those holding the most information. They will be those able to state, for anything they hold, what it is for, who owns it, where it came from and when it goes. For years, data minimisation has been treated as a brake on progress. In reality, it is now becoming one of the reasons some organisations are able to move faster than others.

title: Sustainability efforts could reverse public datacentre backlash
raw_text:
The summer of 2026 will be remembered for datacentres becoming a mainstream issue. Unfortunately, for all the wrong reasons. 

A topic long-confined to IT and infrastructure teams is suddenly being hotly discussed by everyone from acclaimed authors, to drink brands, and the US president. There is even evidence that datacentres may become the defining issue of the approaching US midterms.

While those of us in the industry know that datacentres have quietly underpinned technological innovation for decades, AI has pulled them into a leading role and the limelight has been unflattering. 

There is no getting around the fact that public sentiment on datacentres today is resoundingly negative, with studies showing that around half of Brits now oppose datacentre construction in their local area. In America, that figure is 75%, making it a rare issue that unites opinion across party-political lines.

The public’s opposition to datacentres is representative of a wider anxiety around the environmental impact of increased computing demand, driven by the rise of agentic AI. Their physical presence makes them an obvious focal point for outrage but it is the technology running within them that is driving unsustainable consumption. 

It is up to companies to address the sustainability of their AI roll-outs now before the public backlash extends beyond datacentres to the Large Language Models (LLMs) running within them. Failure to do so could put their investment in AI deployments – and all of the efficiency gains they are yet to realise – at risk.

Sustainability issues drive public backlash 

Studies in the US and UK consistently expose sustainability issues as the driving cause of the datacentre backlash:

  • A YouGov survey showed environmental impact as the main cause of opposition in the UK (cited by 39% of respondents), followed by pressure on energy supply / infrastructure, and water usage concerns.

  • A University of Massachusetts (UMass) poll showed “Environmental Harm and Depletion of Natural Resources” was by far the largest bracket of opposition in the US.

  • Fox News also found that 75% cited concerns such as energy use, water bills and traffic as the main reason they opposed a datacentre in their area.

While there is undeniably work to be done by the hyperscalers to improve sustainability practices and prove environmental responsibility, businesses also need to acknowledge their role in bringing public opinion to a boiling point. 

Datacentres are meeting demand driven by companies that have ramped up computing consumption with little-to-no concern for sustainability. Nearly a third of all cloud usage is wasted on “zombie” resources, which demonstrates the efficiencies that could be gained, the capacity that could be used, and the waste that could be reduced to conserve resources and win back public trust.

This waste is now exacerbated by a rush to deploy agentic AI at scale with the same lack of care. According to data from the British Standards Institute, 62% of businesses say they expect to increase investment in AI this year but only 27% consider their AI footprint in sustainability strategy and reporting. Most companies have no sustainability plan, no commitments, or even a top level number for the impact of their AI usage. 

Companies need to learn the lessons from cloud computing and demonstrate a commitment to adopting AI in an informed and responsible way from the start.

Action companies can take

There are three actions that all businesses that use datacentres can take to play their part in addressing legitimate public concerns around environmental impact:

  • Incentivise computing efficiency: A large part of the 29% of zombie resources are due to a culture where consumption is incentivised and there are few consequences for generating waste. For proof that this attitude has carried into the AI era you need look no further than tokenmaxxing – where exhaustive AI consumption was falsely equated with innovation. Companies including Uber, Amazon, and Meta were among the first to feel the enormous expense of this practice but all companies need to go further to incentivise employees to use AI in a cost- and resource-effective way to reduce environmental and financial waste.

  • Demonstrate sustainable decision making: Companies have the agency to make choices when it comes to datacentres and AI to reduce their environmental footprint. AI providers and models have levels of different environmental impact and organisations can make smart decisions about using the right LLM for the right task, in order to minimise the carbon, energy and water impact of their AI. Intentionality in decision making will go a long way to winning back public trust.

  • Increased public transparency: It has been argued by some commentators that the environmental impact of datacentres is overblown. However, this is not the fault of the public – it is the consequence of a lack of transparency. Obfuscation around water consumption, energy sources, and carbon output, means that it is very easy for public opinion to be swayed by, for example, reports of rising local temperatures, noise pollution, and use of forever chemicals. As companies increase their use of AI, it is within their own interests to be open about the environmental impact of their deployments and methods they are taking to offset adverse effects.

All three of these actions hinge on the availability and use of sustainability data to provide trusted figures that companies’ IT teams can use to identify the greatest areas of environmental impact, take positive actions, and demonstrate progress to the public. 

Datacentres are in the spotlight but AI could be next

While much of the public’s ire has been directed towards the most visible target of datacentres, in reality it is the businesses that run services within them that need to change their practices to reduce waste, improve efficiencies, and ensure datacentre usage grows sustainably.

This has not been a priority for businesses to date. There have been few incentives for companies to be more efficient in their cloud, AI, and datacentre usage and it wasn’t in hyperscalers’ interests to encourage companies to use fewer resources.

But, in the era of AI, there is a lot at stake if companies don’t learn the mistakes from the past and tackle sustainability openly and head on. AI has far more organisational impact than cloud computing as it extends past IT teams and is more reliant on wider employee buy-in. Early studies have shown that environmental responsibility is a major issue for staff, especially younger generations. More than half (53%) of Gen Z employees say that they are concerned about the environmental impact of AI and they are up to four times more likely to list it as an issue than baby boomers.

This isn’t just about awkward questions for executives. It could derail deployment of the “big AI roll-out”. If employees are dissatisfied with answers around ethical concerns about AI usage, leaving licenses unused, and companies facing a lot of cost with very little gain.

Companies should see the datacentre backlash as a bellwether of what is to come if they don’t adopt AI in an informed and responsible way. There is an opportunity now for organisations to create the framework for their AI usage to grow sustainably, where every kilowatt of power leads to maximum output and minimum environmental cost. Those that learn from the lessons of the past and take sustainably seriously will reap the benefits of greater adoption rates, happier staff, and higher ROI for their AI roll-outs.

John Ridd is co-founder and CEO of Greenpixie.

title: Denmark stands against critics of public sector AI plans
raw_text:
Denmark is preparing to give public bodies legal powers to process people’s personal data with artificial intelligence (AI), but critics say the plan undermines data protection and human rights.

While Danish businesses are ranked as Europe’s foremost users of AI, government attempts to use the technology widely in the public sector have been hindered by poor data quality and legal uncertainty, which has deterred municipalities from using AI to improve public services, the Danish government said last year.

The government’s proposed solution – a bill soon to be tabled in parliament – would give public bodies a blanket right to process personal data with AI in pursuit of their legislated service obligations. It would permit them to build and train AI systems, and use those systems to profile people and administer their lives through the provision of public services.

Criticisms include AI potentially increasing the risks of state authorities intruding into people’s lives illegally, offending their data protection and privacy rights, the bill acknowledged.

Despite the risks, the bill is set to waive rules that prevent data collected for one purpose being used for another. That safeguard, and uncertainty about whether laws that allowed public bodies to process data when delivering services extended to AI, has stalled its roll-out.

Legal gap

Doubts were allayed and a legal gap verified in 2023 when Datatilsynet, the Danish Data Protection Agency (DPA), told Copenhagen municipality that existing law gave it a right to use personal data to train an AI system for triaging patients in need of physiotherapy interventions, but not the right to use it. The government drafted the bill to fill the gap. Digital rights campaigners protested that its general permission lacked measures to contain the risks.

“This is a law that says whenever AI is involved, normal rules don’t apply,” Jesper Lund, chairman of Danish legal campaign group IT-Politisk Forening, told Computer Weekly. IT-Pol’s consultation response said the proposed law was so offensive to data protection principles that it should not be tabled in parliament.

“The big irony is that the Danish Data Protection Agency has complained about public authorities using AI because the legal basis wasn’t precise and clear. The government’s response is to grant an even less precise and much broader legal basis. They have been given carte blanche to do what they want,” he said.

“In a rule-of-law society, public authorities cannot do whatever they want. It is not the same as for citizens and companies. For public authorities, anything that is not expressly permitted is not allowed, because we want people to be free of repression from the state,” Lund added.

“If the government has powers of discrimination over you, you should know what they are, and you should have options for redress. You do not want the government taking arbitrary action against you. That is why we have laws,” he said.

IT-Pol and other legal campaign groups are concerned that the government has proposed a broad legal basis for public bodies to use AI in ways that interfere with people’s privacy rights, when European Union law requires such intrusions to have precisely defined circumstances, purposes and safeguards against abuse. It lacks sufficient limits and safeguards and neglects to guarantee that the general provision is necessary or proportionate, according to critics.

Datatilsynet produced a long list of warnings after the first draft bill was published in February. Crucially, the draft provided insufficient legal justification for derogations ministers and public bodies could make from European data protection (GDPR) rights protecting people from state intrusion. A revised draft the government published in September failed to answer most, a data protection official close to the situation told Computer Weekly. It had reflected some, the DPA said on 12 October, when the second consultation closed. An intervening general election annulled the first draft, forcing its reintroduction.

The DPA accepted the general legal basis but found inadequate justification for the bill’s proposed derogations, said the official. That was, notably, AI reuse of personal data collected for other purposes and delegated powers for ministers to exempt whole sectors or systems from obligations to meet people’s data-subject rights.

Rather than neglect the justification for derogating people’s rights, the bill left ministers and public bodies responsible for it. Ministers could justify derogations of data-subject rights only under GDPR Article 23 exceptions, such as public security, crime, health, social security or important financial matters. Failing that, public bodies would have to justify data reuse by doing compatibility assessments. They would still have to do assessments to meet their GDPR obligations anyway, as with any other risky data processing. They would still have to demonstrate a particular system’s processing was necessary and proportionate, and implement safeguards against abuse. The bill just gave them a basis to do that.

The DPA had effectively told the government it had solved a tiny part of the problem, but many remained, the official said. The regulator had meanwhile learned that many public bodies were ready to press go on AI projects once the bill passed, believing it did indeed give them carte blanche to run systems on personal data. So, it devised its consultation response half as a public service announcement to public bodies: the law did not make everything A-OK, and the buck stopped with them. Without an exception, ministers and public bodies would have to provide the missing justification.

Stalled projects

AI projects obstructed for want of legal cover included a system for child welfare cases, and health systems to improve cancer treatment, aid GP diagnosis and identify people at risk of hospitalisation, according to a 2024 analysis of 40 “signature projects” the government designated as test cases.

The government said last year that two-thirds faced legal difficulties, preventing four from being used at all, and others had limited functions. Of 31 health and social care projects, one was operational at the last assessment, and barely half were completed. Technical problems, including widespread poor data quality, often accounted for delays.

Denmark’s IT Industry Association, representing public sector AI suppliers, welcomed the bill, chief consultant Asbjørn Flügge told Computer Weekly. But industry was concerned that leaving responsibility for justifying AI use to ministers could cause fragmentation, with some parts of the public sector becoming more permissive than others.

Denmark, known as a world leader in digital public services, naturally hit these challenges before other countries, said Flügge, whose PhD concerned an AI project to predict long-term unemployment that stalled for want of legal basis. The government appears not to have thought things through, while aspects of GDPR have become outdated and unhelpful. Public opinion of AI has soured since February’s first draft.

“All government’s AI policies and hopes were blocked by its own lack of legal regulation,” said Ida Marie Schrøder, associate professor of technologies in practice at the IT University of Copenhagen, who co-wrote a study of a media storm that led to early Danish attempts to use AI in aid of child protection being cancelled. One, Gladsaxe, intended to detect vulnerable children, became a byword for unacceptable algorithmic practice.

Many of the signature projects were blocked because they were not legal to start with, said Schrøder. “That was lucky for us Danes because no one had a clue what they were developing. And I am afraid they still don’t,” she said.

title: Cooling – not compute – is the binding constraint on the AI factory
raw_text:
The debate about AI infrastructure is dominated by two scarcities: GPUs and electricity. Both matter. But inside the building, a third constraint now decides how much compute a site can actually run, and it is the oldest problem in electronics – getting the heat away from the processor and out of the building. 

Every watt a processor consumes becomes a watt of heat that must be removed, continuously, for the life of the facility. Compute can be bought. Heat rejection has to be engineered.

Let’s start with the scale of the change. A decade ago, a rack drawing 10kW was considered dense. Today's leading AI accelerators – ie, GPUs – dissipate between roughly 70W and more than 1kW per device according to their public datasheets, and rack-scale systems have moved accordingly. A single rack with 72 accelerators is now rated at about 120kW. 

The International Energy Agency estimates that datacentres consumed 415TWh of electricity in 2024 and projects, in its base case, roughly 945TWh by 2030. Nearly every watt of that ends up as heat that someone has to move out of a building.

Air has run out of headroom

Air served the industry well for decades, but it is a poor coolant, and physics does not negotiate. Per unit volume, water carries roughly 3,500x more heat than air for the same temperature rise. At 120kW per rack, cooling with air would mean moving implausible volumes of it. Fan power climbs, noise climbs, and the geometry of fins and heat sinks simply runs out of surface. Air cooling does not fail gradually. Designs cross a threshold beyond which no practical fan or heat sink can hold semiconductor temperatures within their limits, and the newest rack-scale systems sit far beyond that threshold.

That is why the industry's centre of gravity has shifted to liquid – cold plates mounted directly on the devices that dissipate the most power, coolant distribution units at the rack or row level, and a facility loop that carries heat outside. The question for operators is no longer whether liquid cooling will arrive in the AI hall, but how much of the heat it can capture and at what temperature.

Most facilities will not flip overnight. Existing halls built for air are being retrofitted with rear-door heat exchangers and partial liquid loops, and each step helps – but each also confirms the same physics. Retrofitting liquid into a live facility is slow, capital-intensive work, which is why the new generation of AI factories is designed cooling-first, and why older sites face a hard ceiling on the compute they can ever host, whatever their power supply.

Warm water changes the economics

The counterintuitive answer is to run the coolant warmer, not colder. Published reference designs for the next generation of AI factory platforms are now 100% liquid-cooled, with coolant supplied at temperatures up to 45°C. At that level, heat can be rejected to the outside air through dry coolers for much of the year in many climates, without mechanical chillers – and, in the published design figures, with on-site water consumption reduced to near zero where conditions allow. 

Individual operators will make their own choices, but the direction of travel is clear. Coolant temperature has become an efficiency variable in its own right, and the cooling loop is now part of the product architecture rather than the building services.

Cooling also decides geography. A facility in a cool, dry climate can reject heat cheaply for much of the year. One in a hot, humid region, with ambient temperatures of 30°C to 35°C and no free-cooling hours to harvest, pays for every degree of approach temperature in energy and capital. Grid capacity, water availability and heat rejection now sit in the same site-selection spreadsheet, and increasingly they are the deciding rows.

Design for heat first

The cost of getting this wrong is not only energy. A system starved of cooling protects itself by throttling, and a throttled accelerator is capacity that has been bought, installed and powered but cannot be used. Cooling quality shows up directly in useful output per watt – the measure by which AI factories are increasingly judged.

Three habits separate the facilities that scale from the ones that stall. 

  • First, treat cooling as a design input at the silicon, server and rack level – not as a facilities afterthought to be solved once compute is chosen. 

  • Second, measure what matters – device junction temperatures and coolant temperature rise, not just the air temperature of the room. By the time the room is warm, the silicon has been throttling for some time. 

  • Third, design for end-of-life rather than day one. Fouling, pump wear and the next, denser generation of racks all consume margin, and a cooling design with no margin is a capacity limit waiting to be discovered.

The industry spent decades treating cooling as plumbing – necessary, unglamorous, and somebody else's problem. In the AI factory it is none of those things. It is the constraint that determines how much intelligence a building can produce. The organisations that design for heat first will deploy faster than those still designing around it.

Ajay Sekar is a thermal engineer at Nvidia

title: Funding, people and patience: How the UK can become a deeptech leader
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI), digital twinning, quantum, semiconductors – there are a number of technological advancements currently being developed that require a large amount of time, money and resources, having become known in some circles as deeptech.

The UK government has some ambitious plans for these technologies, but how can we ensure this is achieved? 

At a Global Tech Advocates (GTA) event, women who are leaders in deeptech highlighted three important areas to consider: funding, people and patience.

Obtaining funding

The UK government has a lot of hope for the UK’s potential to become a leader in deeptech, having recently announced a £500m Sovereign AI Unit designed to provide venture capital to UK-based AI companies.

Quantum has also been a focus for the UK government, with it announcing it wants the UK to be the first country to deliver quantum computing at scale, investing £1bn to drive research and development to make this a reality.

In fact, Suki Fuller, co-lead of the Tech London Advocates (TLA) Women Leading Tech Group, said we’re currently at an “inflection point”, highlighting government aims for the UK to own 5% of the global chip market by 2030.

But she also cautioned that “momentum doesn’t build itself”, and claimed: “We know what it looks like when opportunities pass, how do we make sure that doesn’t happen again?”

Several speakers explained while government involvement and funding is a step in the right direction, it’s not enough alone to create the tech-led UK the government envisions for the future.

In the words of Janet Collyer, non-executive director and advisor at Mach42: “It will never work if you expect the government to lead. By all means bring them to the table, what is the value of strategic partners? Have them on your board. Nothing happens until somebody sells something.”

Put plainly, Ekaterina Almasque, founding partner, BlankPage Capital, said: “Government and risk doesn’t go together. All these initiatives, they’re admirable, but every time there is something I wonder how it’s going to work, there are so many good intentions behind those initiatives, but in practice we’ve not yet seen a great initiative working.”

Investment and growth needs to come from other areas – venture capital needs to back small businesses looking into how these technologies can be used and developed, firms need to be developing and deploying deeptech, and research needs to be financed and supported.

But one of the factors pointed out by speakers was the difference in the way investment is approached in the UK and Europe versus elsewhere in the world – a large number of startups will be unsuccessful, and the UK’s risk appetite for that is lower.

Almasque said: “Risk capital, the whole model in Europe, doesn’t work because 9/10 ventures will fail and its fine – if we take the risk, we can have more bold outcomes. Nobody knows what will work, but if it works it will save lives.”

Funding for particular projects can be hard to come by, and these issues are exacerbated with deeptech because it’s so experimental and takes a very long time to see results.

Collyer also pointed out that funding is the tip of the iceberg when it comes to building successful deeptech startups.

“The current government has tried to do something, and the thing is what do you do? You don’t just have a helicopter and drop the money down, because they will fail as well,” she said. “It has to be structured.

“Theres a lot of money that is coming into the UK, and the improved relationship with Europe means that we will have funds coming this way as well.”

Collecting the right people

The fear of failure that prevents investment into deeptech is also a cultural issue across the UK technology sector as a whole.

Sue Daley, director of technology and innovation at TechUK, explained: “It’s culture as well, right? Fail fast, pick yourself up and move.

“In the public sector you have to account for the money; in the private sector you have that, it’s a very British thing I think, that shame of failing and therefore not wanting to try again,” she said. “We need to find a solution – how do you change that culture? How do you instil that it’s OK to fail, but it’s picking yourself up and getting going again that’s the important thing.”

Not only does this fear of failure prevent investment in certain types of technology, it also prevents women from shooting their shot for funding, which is an issue when considering female entrepreneurs already receive less funding than their male counterparts.

But Fuller pointed out that women are needed in the deeptech sector as entrepreneurs, advisors and investors – much like the development of other technologies, it’s important to have people from different perspectives and backgrounds working collaboratively on development to ensure technology is suitable for its target uses and audience.

This is especially important for deeptech, which Fuller stated is not “fluffy” tech, but in fact the basis for the future.

She said: “I think sometimes culture has made [women] more risk adverse, but as my grandmother always says, no day is promised, so why not fail today, because you don’t know if you’re going to have tomorrow.

“We have women in the community that are heavily filled with all this knowledge and experience within the deeptech sector, and we are very much siloed. What we want to do is make sure we all know each other because we’re all out there.”

Both Fuller and Clare Schramm, managing director of transaction banking technology platforms at Lloyds Banking Group, went on to say people hoping to take part in the deeptech sector in any capacity need to have the right “mindset”, with Schramm saying: “I think it’s really important getting more of an innovation mindset, tolerating risk, tolerating the potential that a partnership could fail, a business could deviate, that plans may change.”

Zahra Shah, AI and frontier technology expert, has seen people fail without having the right attitude and character, stating: “I’ve seen if you have the wrong kind of character trait for a founder or entrepreneur – no matter how much money they make, no matter how much access to compute they have – if they don’t have the temperament, they’re not going to succeed.”

Investors not only have to believe in the idea and technology they’re investing in, they also have to believe in the people they’re investing in to deliver what has been promised – Collyer explained: “When you talk to most investors, they really start with the team.

“There’s a level of pragmatism that’s coming up, and I see that with investors, and that’s why the team is so important. The tech is proven – that’s good – but the team is the one that’s going to get it over the line. What does it take to be successful?”

Patience is a virtue

The slow speeds deeptech can take to develop often means investment stalls because these projects aren’t delivered as quickly as an investor might like, increasing the feeling of risk, but deeptech takes time, and experts at the Global Tech Advocates event urged having more patience.

One panel member pointed out it can take 15 to 20 years for even the largest companies to perfect a technology, so why rush deeptech ventures?

Schramm said: “Putting [deeptech companies] through the same paces you would put a large enterprise or a FTSE 100 through doesn’t work.

“We have to be able to take more risk, we have to accept the risk, we have to be comfortable we won’t be as mature in some areas but be comfortable there will be a path to risk mitigate.”

Venture capital cannot invest in these technologies and expect a project to be done in a year – it takes “much longer than the noise we hear for the last two, three years” about AI and other emerging technologies, said Harini Gopalakrishnan, founder of TheHaze.

“Having to scale up deeptech really is about playing the long game,” she said.

Not only was patience with deeptech development advised, but Christina Yan Zhang, CEO of The Metaverse Institute, claimed the tech sector needs to have a little more patience with government.

“We need to be a little bit more patient with government,” she said. “We all know the global economy is a little bit slow, not because the government is not working hard, but because we have some uncertainty in the Middle East.

“All governments were overspending during the pandemic to save people’s lives – that’s a medical emergency. In Britain, we have a saying: ‘Keep calm and carry on’. Maybe sometimes we need to be like that towards governments.”

title: Efficient chips cannot save inefficient software
raw_text:
Who is responsible for AI optimisation? Is it those who make the chips, build the infrastructure, and develop the software we use? Is it those who train the LLMs? Or is it the responsibility of those who use AI in their daily lives? 

Semiconductor manufacturers determine the efficiency of the underlying hardware. Cloud and datacentre operators influence power, cooling, and infrastructure utilisation. Model developers decide how large, computationally intensive, and reusable an AI model will be. 

But enterprise architects, developers, and users ultimately determine how often that model is invoked, what information it processes and whether a task requires AI at all. This shared-responsibility model matters because the green IT debate has traditionally concentrated on physical infrastructure. 

Datacentre power usage effectiveness, renewable-energy procurement, server efficiency, and embodied carbon remain critical. But, infrastructure supply is only half the equation. Software creates the demand. The Green Software Foundation now describes sustainable technology explicitly as stretching “from silicon to screen.”

The environmental impact of software comes from three interconnected factors:

  • Energy efficiency. How much electricity does the software consume?

  • Hardware efficiency. How effectively does the software use servers, processors, memory, and storage?

  • Carbon awareness. Do flexible workloads run in locations and time periods with lower-carbon electricity?

These are the principles embedded into the Software Carbon Intensity Specification, which calculates the carbon emissions rate of a software system using operational energy, grid carbon intensity, and the embodied carbon in hardware. 

The specification became ISO/IEC 21031:2024 in March 2024, giving technology leaders a consistent basis for evaluating software during design, development, and deployment rather than treating software emissions as an abstract sustainability issue.

Case studies prove positive green impact of software

One large enterprise described to Forrester that they are proactively coaching engineers to make software development less wasteful and work to analyse code against green-coding principles, explicitly connecting leaner software with lower production energy use. 

The Green Software Foundation now reports seven-plus independent SCI implementations with published results and cites an Autostrade per l'Italia implementation across 60 applications with an average 15.1% CO₂ saving per application. 

Intesa Sanpaolo is another strong case study. Working with NTT DATA, the bank developed a green index for code sustainability and monitors IT energy consumption and carbon emissions. Its monitoring approach uses overall CO₂e and software carbon intensity (SCI), with the objective of finding opportunities to optimise software and hardware usage. 

These figures and efforts should not be treated as benchmarks. But it demonstrates that code-level interventions can produce measurable operational improvements rather than merely theoretical benefits.

The challenges for software leaders

In partnership with software development, architecture, FinOps, and sustainability leaders, CIOs and software leaders must confront several practical barriers to improving software sustainability. Some, such as challenges to infrastructure visibility and inconsistent cloud data, cannot be fully solved by an individual enterprise. Standards and measurement tools are still evolving, and optimisation will always involve trade-offs with budgeting, performance, security, resilience, cost, and other business decisions. The goal is to not let perfection be the enemy of good, and start with the available data, and make an iterative plan for best practices.

These are some of the challenges:

1. Software emissions are difficult to isolate. Modern applications operate across containers, serverless services, shared cloud infrastructure, managed databases, user devices, and third-party APIs. Allocating server-level energy consumption to an individual application or transaction remains difficult, particularly when the organisation does not control the underlying infrastructure.

2. Carbon data is inconsistent. Cloud providers publish environmental information using different boundaries, methodologies, and reporting schedules. This remains a problem since the advent of cloud. The Real-Time Energy and Carbon Standard for Cloud Providers seeks to normalise regional energy and carbon information across the three largest public-cloud platforms. The standard includes data fields covering power and water efficiency, carbon-free energy, and multiple forms of carbon intensity. Another resource for comparing cloud footprint across hyperscalers is the open source Cloud Carbon Footprint.org

3. Optimisation can conflict with other requirements. Moving a workload to a “cleaner” region may introduce latency, data-sovereignty, or resilience concerns. Delaying a batch process may reduce emissions but violate an operational deadline. Refactoring code may improve energy efficiency while creating security, quality or maintainability risks. Academic research also acknowledges that the practical benefit of temporal and geographic workload shifting can be constrained by capacity, latency requirements, privacy restrictions and workload characteristics. Therefore, sustainability belongs in architecture trade-off decisions, not in an isolated environmental checklist

4. Efficiency can stimulate more demand. Lower-cost AI can encourage greater use. For AI, reductions in the energy required for each inference can be overwhelmed by rapid growth in inference volume. CIOs must track intensity and total consumption. A carbon-per-transaction figure is useful, but it does not guarantee that the application’s absolute footprint is declining.

5. Developers lack incentives and usable feedback. Development teams are measured on accurate functionality, reliability, security, cost, and delivery speed. Energy consumption rarely appears in acceptance criteria or engineering scorecards. Without telemetry in development and production, engineers cannot see whether a design decision improved or worsened environmental performance.

Start with measurement

To get started, CIOs can take three simple steps: measure, optimise, and govern. 

  • Measure energy, carbon, and compute demand per transaction, user, or AI inference, and also track that the application’s total consumption to ensure efficiency gains are not erased by rising use. Use the Software Carbon Intensity Specification, and other tools such as the Green Software Foundation’s Impact Framework or Red Hat’s Kepler. 
  • Optimise inefficient code and infrastructure before shifting flexible workloads with the Carbon Aware SDK. 
  • Govern the results through architecture, FinOps, procurement and AI oversight. 

Sustainable software starts when computational efficiency becomes a core engineering requirement, not an optional environmental feature.

Abhijit Sunil is a senior analyst with Forrester.

Read more about software carbon footprint

  • Green IT: Taking responsibility for software’s physical footprint. Green IT must look beyond physical datacentres to software efficiency. Optimising code, data retention, and architecture reduces energy demand and hardware churn
  • Software architecture as the first line of climate defence. True digital sustainability requires addressing software waste. Refactoring bloated code cuts computational overhead, lowering enterprise energy consumption and hardware churn
summary:
Who is responsible for AI optimisation? Is it those who make the chips, build the infrastructure, and develop the software we use? Is it those who train the LLMs? Or is it the responsibility of those who use AI in their daily lives? 

Semiconductor manufacturers determine the efficiency of the underlying hardware.
